name: Tahltan
confidence_why: Alderete & Bob's 2005 corpus study of a Telegraph Creek speaker finds primary stress on the stem syllable in every noun and about 88% of verbs, agreeing with Cook 1972 and with Nater's own 2006 statement that the verb stem is stressed unless a stress-attracting prefix intervenes; the only dissent is Nater 1989, who argued from Iskut data that stress is phonemic and non-iterative, an older position that Alderete & Bob address directly and that may partly reflect a different speech community.

catalog_quote: These predominant patterns support the following generalizations: 1. the stem syllable is always stressed ... 2. there is always a stressed syllable that precedes the stem syllable 3. in contexts where there is more than one syllable preceding the stem, stress is assigned on alternating syllables counting from the stem syllable Generalizations 1. and 2. are strong enough to bring about stress clash (3ab), despite the avoidance of two adjacent stressed syllables implicit in generalization 3. ... Thus one salient observation is that there is a strong tendency for primary stress to fall on the stem. This tendency is absolute in both possessed and unpossessed nouns. The only exceptions to this trend are in verbs ... Finally, we examine briefly the position of main stress. sweep_summary: All three works with stress in the title are one work: Alderete & Bob, 'A corpus-based approach to Tahltan stress' — the Glottolog text entry, its Benjamins DOI record (Crossref: Athabaskan Prosody, pp. 369-391, issued 2005-10-26), and the ANLA archive copy CN002AB2002 of the February-2002 manuscript. The ANLA record (downloaded via the archive's Drupal API; Glottolog's URL is dead) describes it as 'ca. 26 (2 per page)', which matches the held author-site preprint ('Version: February 2002', 27 ms pages 2-up). That preprint is the catalog's deciding source, already held by the project and now copied into our check folder; re-read, it confirms the set by morphology coding (stem syllable always stressed, absolute in nouns, obligatory pre-stem stress, alternating secondaries; main stress last in 85%). No new Tahltan stress literature surfaced: Crossref bibliographic search for 'Tahltan stress' returns only A&B 2005 and Cook 1972; archive.org has nothing; Two corrections for our check store's list of works to obtain: Cook 1972 is doi:10.1086/465221 (not 465223 = Walker, Zuni) and Nater 1989 is doi:10.1086/466103 (not 466102 = Thompson, Koyukon); both remain paywalled (uchicago 403). Held Alderete & Blenkiron 2014 synopsis sec. 2.3 and Nater 2006 (stem stress in finite verbs unless a stress-attracting prefix overrides) agree with and refine the classification. Bob 1999 UBC thesis still unreachable (UBC bot-block). Suggested action: none for the classification; fix the two DOIs and the dead ANLA URL in the per-language bibliography.

new_statements.quote: In general, we have found that there is a strong correlation between stem position and primary stress, which is consistent with Cook's findings. Furthermore, the only exceptions to this generalization are in verbs, which is also true of Nater's exceptions to the stress-to-stem generalization. Concerning stress and rhythm, our results compare to Cook's in that stress is, by and large, rhythmically distributed in the sense that two adjacent syllables of equal stress rank are strongly avoided. However, as shown in 3.3 and 3.4, there are certain important contexts where stress clash is permitted

new_statements.reading: Primary stress falls on the (morphological) stem syllable — absolute in nouns, with a small verb-only residue — and secondary stresses alternate leftward from it with an obligatory pre-stem stress; syllable weight plays only a marginal role (CVV may attract stress off the stem). The authors explicitly reconcile Cook 1972 (stem + alternating rule) and Nater 1989 (phonemic, non-iterative stress) in favour of a morphologically anchored, rhythmically distributed system. This is the catalog's own deciding source read again in full; the passage quoted here is its summary section, which complements the sec. 3.1 generalizations already in the record.

readall_conflicts: Neither listed work could be opened, so no new primary statement was obtained and no new conflict arises. The known disagreement in the literature (reported secondhand by Alderete & Bob 2002 and the Alderete et al. 2005 bibliography, both held by the project) is Cook 1972 (Lower Post speaker: stress predictable, on the stem syllable and alternating syllables from it) versus Nater 1989 (Iskut: stress phonemic/unpredictable, non-iterative, only compounds carry more than one stress); the catalog's deciding source (Alderete & Bob) resolves this in favour of stem-anchored primary stress with rhythmic secondary stresses and a small verb-only residue. Cook's own text was not read here, so his exact wording remains unverified.

audit.reasoning: The record rests on the dedicated, most recent and most extensive study of Tahltan stress (Alderete & Bob 2005, corpus of 370 tallied words), held as the author-site preprint with a clean column-split text; every fragment of the deciding quotation, the domain quote and the exceptions quote is verbatim at the stated ms pages (6, 8, 11, 13, 14). The held Alderete & Blenkiron 2014 synopsis agrees. The annotated Tahltan bibliography (downloaded now) and Alderete 2005 (downloaded now) both confirm that the stress literature consists of Cook 1972, Nater 1989 and A&B, with A&B reconciling the other two; The set by morphology coding (stem syllable stressed, absolute in nouns, ~88% in 4-syllable words; main stress = last stress in 85%) matches the source

sources.citation: Alderete, John & Amber Blenkiron. 2014. Tahltan grammar synopsis. Ms., Simon Fraser University. (held secondary; not in the list of works with stress in the title)
sources.quote: Main stress rule: assign main stress to the stem syllable (generally final syllable, but exceptionally the penult) and secondary stress to alternating syllables counting backwards from the main stress. Additionally, there must be a stress on a pre-stem syllable, which can lead to two adjacent stressed syllables if there is only one pre-stem syllable.
sources.locator: sec. 2.3 Suprasegmentals, (14) Stress assignment rule, ms pp. 7-8
sources.note: Fieldworker's own grammar synopsis restating A&B 2005 as a rule: main stress on the stem, alternating secondaries leftward, obligatory pre-stem stress; phonetic correlates higher F0, loudness, duration. Agrees with the catalog's set by morphology coding.

sources.citation: Nater, Hank F. 2006. Athabascan verb stem structure: Tahltan. In G. Rowicka & E. Carlin (eds.), What's in a verb?, 53-72. Utrecht: LOT. (held, open access; not in the list of works with stress in the title)
sources.quote: In finite verbs not containing a stress-attracting prefix (cf. fn. 3 and 16), the stem receives the stress. [...] Where two stress-attracting non-pronominal prefixes occur in sequence, location of stress is determined by the leftmost such prefix.
sources.note: Nater's later (Iskut-based) statement: stem stress is the default in finite verbs, overridden by lexically 'stress-attracting' prefixes, the leftmost winning when two co-occur. This is the same verb-only exception class A&B report (chart (7): 7/50 verbs without primary stem stress) and refines the catalog's exceptions note with a morphological mechanism; it does not change the classification.
